metadata.title: Intraocular Foreign Body Management, Acute Referral Centre
metadata.summary: This guideline covers the assessment and acute management of suspected intraocular foreign bodies at an acute referral centre. It addresses injury history, ocular examination, imaging, precautions when globe rupture is suspected, and preparation for surgery. It also specifies initial protective measures, antibiotics and tetanus-related care.

decision_rules: Promptly assess suspected IOFB for ocular and other injuries, then establish a management plan.
When an IOFB is not readily visible, use imaging to determine the location and number of foreign bodies; more than 1 IOFB may be present. CT with 1mm slices is required in most suspected cases.
Discuss subsequent management and theatre arrangements with the senior on-call clinician or ARC consultant.

conditions.name: Intraocular Foreign Bodies (IOFB)
conditions.description: A suspected intraocular foreign body requires assessment of ocular injuries and any other injuries. The entry site and the foreign body may not be visible, and more than 1 IOFB may be present.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The patient may have no symptoms or may report a change in VA, pain, pain with eye movement, photophobia, diplopia, floaters, photopsia or other visual disturbance. Possible findings include globe rupture or penetration, extrusion of intraocular contents, reduced IOP relative to the other eye, scleral haemorrhage, marked chemosis, a visible foreign body, a corneal wound or localised oedema, a shallow or collapsed anterior chamber, hyphaema, an irregular pupil or iris defect, lens opacity or injury, vitreous haemorrhage, and retinal haemorrhage or detachment. Lens dislocation is rare. If an IOFB is found, signs of infection may include hypopyon, anterior chamber activity or vitreous veils, particularly when it has been present for more than 6 hours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish the injury mechanism, foreign-body details, use or non-use of protective eye wear, full medical and ophthalmic history, tetanus status, time of last meal and visual or ocular symptoms.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An absence of symptoms does not exclude IOFB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess ocular injury and inspect the anterior and posterior segments for an entry site, foreign body, haemorrhage and other signs of injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess the iris for abnormalities before dilatation. A peripheral area of corneal oedema may suggest an IOFB in the anterior chamber angle. Neither an unseen entry site nor an unseen foreign body excludes IOFB. If the history and examination remain suggestive, possible concealed locations include the anterior chamber angle, behind the iris, the anterior vitreous or retina, and beneath retinal haemorrhage. Do not perform scleral indentation or gonioscopy if globe rupture is suspected.

diagnostic_workup.test: IOP comparison with the other eye
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify an IOP difference suggestive of ocular injury.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A lower IOP than in the other eye is a possible sign of IOFB.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During anterior segment assessment of possible IOFB.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result is a possible sign of IOFB.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Look for hypopyon, anterior chamber activity and vitreous veils.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: If an IOFB is identified, particularly when it has been present for more than 6 hours.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine the location and number of all IOFBs.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Imaging is needed unless the IOFB is readily visible; CT scan is required in most suspected cases.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Use 1mm slices. Small IOFBs or plastic may be missed.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The guideline considers it rarely useful and probably best avoided during initial assessment. Avoid it with obvious globe rupture or a collapsed anterior chamber; do not perform it if examination without globe compression cannot be assured.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Small IOFBs, especially wood or vegetation, may be missed; gas or air may be mistaken for an IOFB.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be useful if CT is not immediately available.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: They are poor at detecting and locating IOFBs.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Contraindicated when a metallic IOFB cannot be excluded.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL GUIDELINE
document_sections.content: Disease-specific treatment guidance supports, rather than replaces, clinical judgement. Its applicability depends on the individual patient. In people with multiple morbidities or frailty, clinicians should consider the risks of harmful polypharmacy and greater susceptibility to adverse drug reactions. When discussion with the patient or carer identifies good reasons to depart from the guideline, recording those reasons and informing others involved in care is good practice.

document_sections.heading: Intraocular Foreign Bodies Management (IOFB) in Acute Referral Centre
document_sections.content: Every patient with a suspected IOFB needs prompt evaluation of ocular injuries and any other injuries, followed by an appropriate management plan.

document_sections.heading: The Following Features of History and Examination Should be Assessed
document_sections.content: History should cover the injury mechanism, details of the foreign body, whether protective eyewear was used, complete medical and ophthalmic history, tetanus status, and the time of the last meal. A patient may have no symptoms. Ask about a change in VA, pain, pain with eye movement, photophobia, diplopia, floaters, photopsia and other visual disturbance. An entry wound is not always visible. Anterior-segment findings suggesting IOFB include evident globe rupture or penetration, with or without extrusion of intraocular contents; lower IOP than in the other eye; scleral haemorrhage or marked chemosis together with a suggestive history; and a visible FB in the sclera, cornea, anterior chamber or posterior chamber. Other findings include a corneal wound positive on Seidel testing with 2% fluorescein, focal corneal oedema that may indicate an angle-lodged IOFB when peripheral, a shallow or collapsed anterior chamber, hyphaema, an irregular pupil, an iris defect seen directly or by retroillumination, and focal lens opacity, a wound traversing the lens or, rarely, lens dislocation. Assess the iris for these abnormalities before dilatation. Posterior-segment findings include vitreous haemorrhage and retinal haemorrhage or detachment; the IOFB itself may be visible or hidden. Do not use scleral indentation or gonioscopy if globe rupture is suspected. If an IOFB is found, assess for infection, including hypopyon, anterior-chamber activity and vitreous veils, particularly when it has been present for more than 6 hours. If history and examination remain suggestive despite no IOFB being found, possible concealed locations include the anterior-chamber angle, behind the iris, the anterior vitreous or retina, and beneath retinal haemorrhage.

document_sections.heading: Further Assessment
document_sections.content: Imaging is needed unless the IOFB is readily visible. A suspected case may contain more than 1 IOFB, so imaging should establish the position and number of all foreign bodies. CT scan with 1mm slices is required for most suspected cases, although it can miss small IOFBs or plastic. B-scan ultrasound is seldom useful in practice: it may overlook small IOFBs, especially wood or vegetation, and gas or air can be mistaken for an IOFB. It is probably best avoided during initial assessment. Avoid it when the globe is clearly ruptured or the anterior chamber has collapsed, and do not perform it unless examination without globe compression can be assured. Plain X-rays identify and locate IOFBs poorly but may help when CT is not immediately available. MRI is contraindicated if a metallic IOFB cannot be ruled out. Take clinical photographs if possible. Discuss further care and theatre arrangements with the senior clinician on call or consultant in ARC. If transfer to theatre will be significantly delayed, consider intravitreal antibiotics on the ward. Once globe rupture or an IOFB is suspected or confirmed, every case requires an eye shield; admission to Ward 1C, Gartnavel General Hospital; preparation for theatre, including nil by mouth and GA assessment; anti-tetanus toxoid when indicated; Ciprofloxacin 750mg BD; and preservative free chloramphenicol 0.5% QDS. The consultant responsible should obtain surgical consent and discuss prognosis with the patient.

rows:
Signs suggestive of possible IOFB – (N.B. entry site may not always be visible) Anterior Segment

•Obvious globe rupture / penetratration ± extrusion of intraocular contents

•Reduced IOP compared to other eye

•Haemorrhage over sclera or significant chemosis along with suggestive history

•Visible FB embedded in sclera or cornea or in anterior or posterior chamber

•Seidel positive corneal wound with 2% fluorescein

•Cornea – localised oedema. If at periphery may suggest IOFB lodged in angle

•Anterior chamber – shallow / collapsed / hyphaema

•Iris – irregular pupil / visible iris defect / defect visible by retroilluminaion

•Lens – localised opacity / through and through wound / dislocation (rarely) Posterior Segment. NB – Iris to be assessed for above abnormalities before dilatation

•Vitreous – haemorrhage

•Retina – haemorrhage / detachment

•IOFB may or may not be visible !Do not perform scleral indentation or gonioscopy if globe rupture suspected!
